findings.quote: An exception is a compound with a polyatomic ion made of two or more atoms.
findings.problem: This general statement is false. It says a compound with a polyatomic ion is an exception to the rule that an ionic formula already shows the simplest atom ratio. Most such compounds are not exceptions: CaCO3 (used in this lesson's own Example #5), Na2SO4 and NH4Cl are already in simplest whole-number ratio. Only some, such as Na2O2 (peroxide, NaO), are exceptions, where the subscripts share a common factor. Every polyatomic ion has two or more atoms, so the added words do not narrow it. A student taught this would misjudge which ionic formulas reduce. It came in with the fix for the Sol-audit Blocker and goes too far the other way.
findings.source: IUPAC Gold Book, empirical formula (simplest whole-number ratio of atoms); NIST Chemistry WebBook: sodium peroxide Na2O2, calcium carbonate CaCO3; content-checklist.md B01; reader-rules.md, Added after the Sol audit

findings.quote: Ionic compounds have no separate molecules, so they have no molecular formula.
findings.problem: This paragraph has four sentences, over the limit of three. The paragraph that begins "To find the molecular formula, divide the compound's molar mass" also has four sentences.
